synopsis: The research treats build, buy and partner as vendor-neutral alternatives, but identifies credibility—not tool choice—as the decisive risk in selecting an off-road automatic-braking validation toolchain [f297, f200]. For a manufacturer with no virtual-testing capability and nine months before hardware, it recommends a hybrid: retain the operating-domain definition, scenario catalog and correlation data internally, license or co-develop machine physics, and engage a partner for the first correlated sensor model [f8258, f8342]. Expert judgment says a newcomer starting in October 2026 can build a narrow toolchain for the first-release envelope by reusing commercial or open-source simulators rather than writing them from scratch; quick prototypes should not be confused with safety-credible capability [f1591, f8742]. Open-source development offers low license costs but high internal labor and responsibility for credibility evidence, while an integrated commercial stack reduces integration burden without eliminating substantial domain-modeling and correlation work [f16128, f16129, f8748]. Partner-led delivery may be fastest and address the 2027 deadline, but lasting control depends on contracts and knowledge transfer; the booklet recommends clear ownership clauses, editable technical deliverables and open-format export to limit dependency [f16133, f16139, f8764, f16134, f16137, f13217]. No independent 2024–2026 benchmark establishes total cost, headcount or time to a first useful result, and the available vendor cases are qualitative rather than controlled measurements, so the preferred hybrid is a judgment rather than a quantitatively demonstrated winner [f8734, f8315, f16136, f8342].
